opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly I think the term has become a bit overloaded. Right now, when people say "world model," they might mean a video generation model, a simulator for robotics, a game engine you can interact with, or even just a large language model that seems to know a lot of facts about the world. Those are quite different things.

For me, the essence of a world model is not generating pretty pixels. It's about having an internal representation that captures how the world works: what objects are, how they persist, how they interact, what happens when you take an action. It's a predictive model, but the prediction should happen in a space that's meaningful, not necessarily in raw pixel space. If you can generate a beautiful video but the model doesn't understand that a cup falling off a table will break, or that an object behind a wall still exists, then I wouldn't really call that a world model. It's a very good renderer.

So I'd say there are a few key ingredients. First, perception, or representation: you need to see the world well and abstract it in the right way. This is where my background in visual representation learning comes in. I think we've underestimated how important good representations are, and a lot of current generative work kind of skips that step. Second, dynamics: understanding how states evolve over time, especially conditioned on actions. Third, and this is often missing, the model should be useful for something: planning, reasoning, decision-making. A world model exists to let an agent imagine "what if" before acting, the way humans do.

There's also a philosophical piece. Language models learn from text, which is already a compressed, human-curated description of the world. That's powerful, but it's secondhand. A real world model has to learn from the much messier, higher-bandwidth signal of sensory experience, the way a baby or an animal does. A cat has a pretty good world model without any language at all. So to me, building world models is really about going back to that more fundamental kind of intelligence: grounded, spatial, physical, and predictive. I think that's one of the most important open problems in AI right now, and we're still quite early.

r001.rationale: The response lists planning and reasoning as uses for a world model, but does not present them as the same concept.

r002.rationale: It defines a world model as an internal representation of how the world works, including how states and objects evolve, that supports predictions.

r003.rationale: It says the model lets an agent imagine what might happen before acting and supports planning and decision-making, communicating that predictions inform action.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question to open with, and I'll admit the term has become quite muddy, so let me start with what I think the essence actually is.

To me, a world model is fundamentally about prediction and understanding, not about generation. When people hear "world model" today, they often picture a video generator producing beautiful, photorealistic clips. That's a very natural association, because the models that got the most attention, things like Sora or Genie, are generative. But I think that conflates the output with the purpose. The point of a world model is that an agent, whether a robot, a human, or an AI system, needs some internal representation of how the world works so it can anticipate what happens next and plan accordingly. The model is in service of acting in the world.

If you look at how humans do it, we obviously don't render pixels in our heads when we reach for a cup. We have something much more abstract. We know the cup has weight, that it will fall if we let go, that liquid inside will spill. That representation is compressed, structured, and tied to our ability to act. So I'm a bit skeptical that the right path is to model every pixel of the future. Generating pixels is an incredibly expensive way to do prediction, and most of that detail is irrelevant for decision making. The pattern on the tablecloth doesn't matter for picking up the cup.

That said, I don't want to dismiss generative approaches entirely. There's a real argument that if you can generate the world faithfully, you must have understood something about it. Generation is a very strong test of understanding. And practically, video generation gives us a scalable training signal. We have enormous amounts of video, and predicting future frames is a self-supervised objective that doesn't need labels. So I see it as one path to learning the representation, not the end goal itself.

The second piece of the essence, for me, is that a world model has to be about the physical, spatial, dynamic world, not just about language. Large language models are remarkable, and in some sense they contain a kind of world model, but it's a world model learned through text, which is a human-filtered, lossy description of reality. Text tells you what people bothered to write down. It doesn't tell you what it feels like for a ball to roll off a table, or how a scene looks from a different angle. There's a huge amount of knowledge about the world that's never been verbalized, because it's too obvious for anyone to write about. Vision and interaction are how you get at that.

And this connects to something I care a lot about, which is that visual understanding has been somewhat neglected in the current paradigm. People treat vision as a peripheral input to a language model, something you tokenize and feed in. I think that's backwards for world modeling. Spatial understanding, three-dimensional structure, object permanence, physical dynamics, these should be first-class. Our own work on representation learning, and more recently on how to get visual representations that are actually useful for spatial reasoning rather than just for captioning, is trying to push in that direction.

So if I had to compress all of that into one sentence, I'd say a world model is a learned, internal, predictive representation of how the world evolves and responds to action, and the measure of its quality is not how pretty its outputs are but how well it supports understanding and decision making. The field is still arguing about the architecture, whether it's latent prediction, pixel prediction, or something hybrid, and honestly I think that debate is healthy. We haven't solved it yet. But I'd encourage people not to get too attached to the generative framing just because it produces the most impressive demos.

r001.rationale: The response connects prediction to planning and decision making, but does not present planning and reasoning as the same concept.

r002.rationale: It describes a world model as an internal representation of how the world works that lets an agent anticipate what happens next.

r003.rationale: It says the representation helps an agent plan accordingly and supports decision making, tying predictions to action.

astra-6.text:
I think the essence of a world model is learning how the world evolves, including how it changes in response to our actions. Given what I’ve observed so far, and an action I might take, can I anticipate what happens next?

That’s different from simply recognizing what’s in an image. If I see a cup on a table, recognizing the cup is one thing. Understanding that pushing it toward the edge might make it fall requires some model of the dynamics. And because observations are incomplete, that model also needs to represent uncertainty. There may be several plausible outcomes.

The interesting question is what the model needs to represent internally. Does it need to predict every pixel? Maybe not. For a robot trying to pick up that cup, its position, shape, and interaction with the hand may matter much more than the exact texture of the table. So I wouldn’t define a world model by whether it generates realistic video. Video generation can be a way to learn or demonstrate prediction, but visual realism alone doesn’t tell us whether the model understands the consequences of an action.

For me, the central idea is a representation that supports prediction and, ultimately, decision-making. Can you use it to consider possible actions, anticipate their consequences, and then check those expectations against what actually happens? That’s where a world model becomes useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prediction, action, and decision-making, but does not present planning and reasoning as the same concept.

r002.rationale: It defines a world model as a representation of how the world evolves and responds to actions, enabling predictions about what happens next.

r003.rationale: It says the representation supports decision-making by considering possible actions and anticipating their consequences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essence of a world model is learning how the world works well enough to predict what might happen next, including what happens when you take an action. It’s more than recognizing what’s in an image. You need some understanding of how things relate, how they change over time, and which changes your actions can cause.

For example, if I push a cup toward the edge of a table, can the model anticipate that it might fall—even before seeing it fall? And can it use that prediction to choose a different action? That connection between perception, prediction, and action is what makes a world model useful.

I wouldn’t define it by whether it generates realistic video. That can be one way to learn or demonstrate a world model, but visual realism alone doesn’t tell us whether the model understands the underlying dynamics. The deeper question is whether it captures the information needed to reason about possible futures and make decisions.

r001.rationale: The response links perception, prediction, and action, but it does not present planning and reasoning as the same concept.

r002.rationale: It describes learning how the world and its dynamics work, including how things relate and change, to predict possible futures.

r003.rationale: It explicitly asks whether predictions can be used to choose a different action.
